concept.name: Database Sharding & Range Partitioning
concept.tagline: Horizontally partition massive database tables across multiple database instances using shard keys.

spark.summary: Database sharding is the horizontal data partitioning architecture that splits a monolithic database into multiple independent physical database instances (shards), distributing storage capacity, write IOPS, and RAM buffer pools across independent compute nodes.
spark.keyTakeaway: The Sharding Key is an irreversible architectural foundation: choose a key that distributes write traffic uniformly, eliminates cross-shard distributed joins, and matches your core query access patterns.

concept.whyItMatters: Relational databases hit physical hardware ceilings on single instances: write IOPS bottleneck on disk controllers, connection limits exhaust CPU, and datasets outgrow available server RAM. Sharding enables near-linear horizontal scaling beyond hardware limits.
whenToUse: Total dataset size exceeds 1-2 Terabytes and active working sets no longer fit within single-server RAM.
Write transaction throughput exceeds single-instance database disk IOPS and connection limits (> 10,000 writes/sec).
Multi-tenant enterprise SaaS applications requiring complete physical data isolation per enterprise customer.
Geographic data residency requirements where user records must reside within regional geographic boundaries.
whenNotToUse: Early-stage applications where the database fits comfortably on a vertically scaled cloud RDS instance.
Workloads requiring frequent complex cross-table SQL joins and cross-table aggregations (e.g. ad-hoc analytics).
When read scaling can be solved via read replicas, indexing optimizations, and Redis caching.
keyPoints: Sharding Key Selection: Must have high cardinality and even distribution to prevent hot partitions. Common keys: user_id, tenant_id, or composite hashes.
Hash-Based Sharding: Computes shard_id = MurmurHash3(sharding_key) mod N. Guarantees uniform data distribution, but adding new shards requires complex rebalancing.
Range-Based Sharding: Partitions data by continuous ranges (e.g. user_id 1-1M to Shard 1). Supports fast range scans, but vulnerable to write hotspots on the latest range.
Consistent Hashing with Virtual Nodes: Distributes shards across a cryptographic ring, minimizing data movement to 1/N keys during cluster expansion.
Cross-Shard Query Penalty: Queries lacking the sharding key must broadcast (scatter-gather) across all shards, multiplying database load.

examples.title: User-ID Sharded E-Commerce Orders
examples.scenario: An e-commerce platform with 50 million users shards order data by customer user_id across 16 database shards.
examples.outcome: Customer order history lookups query exactly 1 shard with 5ms latency, achieving 80,000 writes/sec across the cluster.

examples.title: Tenant-Based B2B SaaS Isolation
examples.scenario: A B2B cloud ERP partitions enterprise customer data by organization tenant_id.
examples.outcome: Large enterprise customers run on dedicated shards without noisy-neighbor interference affecting smaller tenants.

tradeOffs.pro: Hash-based sharding provides mathematically uniform write distribution, eliminating write hotspots.
tradeOffs.con: Hash-based sharding destroys range query efficiency; a query for a date range requires querying every shard in the cluster.

tradeOffs.factor: Application-Level Routing vs Sharding Middleware (Vitess / Citus)
tradeOffs.pro: Application-level routing provides full code transparency without opaque proxy overhead.
tradeOffs.con: Application-level routing clutters business code with shard resolution logic and connection pool management.

tradeOffs.factor: Horizontal Sharding vs Vertical Hardware Scaling
tradeOffs.pro: Horizontal sharding provides theoretically unbounded throughput and storage expansion.
tradeOffs.con: Horizontal sharding introduces massive operational complexity: schema migrations, backup coordination, and rebalancing.

failureModes.name: The Celebrity Key Hotspot (Data Skew)
failureModes.description: A social network shards by user_id. A celebrity account with 50M followers receives thousands of comments per second, overloading Shard 4 while other shards sit idle.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement Salted Composite Keys for high-volume entities: shard_key = hash(user_id + "_" + (post_id % 10)), distributing comments across 10 shards.

failureModes.name: Scatter-Gather Query Exhaustion
failureModes.description: A frontend feature queries orders by order_status without user_id. The proxy sends the query to all 32 shards simultaneously, saturating connection pools across the entire fleet.
failureModes.mitigation: Build secondary global lookup indexes in DynamoDB or Elasticsearch that map order_status to user_ids before querying the sharded database.

failureModes.name: Cross-Shard Distributed Deadlocks
failureModes.description: A multi-shard transaction attempts to update rows on Shard 1 and Shard 2 concurrently with another transaction in reverse order, locking connection pools.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict single-shard transactional boundaries and use asynchronous Sagas or two-phase commit (2PC) sparingly.

commonMistakes: Choosing a low-cardinality sharding key (e.g. country_code), creating massive imbalanced shards for large countries.
Failing to plan for cluster resharding before databases reach 80% disk capacity.
Executing cross-shard joins inside application loops (N+1 query anti-pattern), causing catastrophic latency spikes.

deepDive.markdownContent:
## 📖 Operational Architecture of Database Sharding

Sharding is the process of breaking up a massive database into smaller, faster, more manageable pieces called shards. Each shard is an autonomous database instance holding a disjoint subset of the total dataset.

```architecture
{
  "view": "high-level",
  "title": "Distributed Sharding Routing Architecture",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "apps", "label": "Application Workers", "type": "client" },
    { "id": "router", "label": "Sharding Router / Proxy (Vitess / Citus / Hash)", "type": "gateway" },
    { "id": "shard1", "label": "Shard 1 (User IDs hash 0-3)", "type": "database" },
    { "id": "shard2", "label": "Shard 2 (User IDs hash 4-7)", "type": "database" },
    { "id": "shard3", "label": "Shard 3 (User IDs hash 8-11)", "type": "database" },
    { "id": "shard4", "label": "Shard 4 (User IDs hash 12-15)", "type": "database" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "apps", "to": "router", "label": "SELECT * WHERE user_id = 9482" },
    { "from": "router", "to": "shard2", "label": "Direct Shard Query (Hash matches Shard 2)" },
    { "from": "apps", "to": "router", "label": "SELECT * WHERE status = 'PENDING' (No Key)" },
    { "from": "router", "to": "shard1", "label": "Scatter-Gather Broadcast (1/4)" },
    { "from": "router", "to": "shard2", "label": "Scatter-Gather Broadcast (2/4)" },
    { "from": "router", "to": "shard3", "label": "Scatter-Gather Broadcast (3/4)" },
    { "from": "router", "to": "shard4", "label": "Scatter-Gather Broadcast (4/4)" }
  ]
}
```

---

### ⚙️ Sharding Key Selection Criteria

The sharding key determines where every row lives. Evaluating candidate keys requires analyzing three factors:

1. **Cardinality**: Must have millions of unique values. Never shard on low-cardinality attributes like `status` or `country`.
2. **Distribution Uniformity**: Hash of the key should distribute rows evenly across all shards, avoiding celebrity hotspot nodes.
3. **Query Co-location**: Frequently joined tables (e.g. `users` and `orders`) should share the same sharding key (`user_id`) so joins occur locally within a single shard instance.

caseStudy.solution: Sharded Cassandra/ScyllaDB cluster using channel_id as partition key.
caseStudy.impact: Sub-10ms message retrieval across billions of daily messages.

relationships.description: Shard routers use consistent hashing to route queries to correct database shards.

questions.title: Shard Key Hotspot Prevention
questions.prompt: Why is selecting a low-cardinality column like 'country_code' as a primary database shard key considered a dangerous architectural pitfall?

options.text: Low-cardinality keys require double the RAM per shard node.
options.explanation: Low cardinality affects data distribution across shards, not per-node RAM allocation.

options.text: Low-cardinality keys create severe data skew, concentrating millions of records onto a few hotspot shards while leaving others underutilized.
options.explanation: Correct! Low cardinality forces large volumes of traffic onto single hotspot shard databases.

rubric.excellent: Explains data skew and un-balanced traffic distribution caused by low-cardinality shard keys.
rubric.gap: Confuses cardinality with memory allocation.

questions.sampleSolution: Low-cardinality keys like country_code force all data for large nations onto single hotspot shards. Use high-cardinality keys like user_id.
questions.explanation: High cardinality keys combined with uniform hash functions guarantee even row distribution across N database shards.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Shard by tenant_id using a dedicated Shard Router service backed by Redis. Colocate all relational tables for a given tenant on the same physical database shard to enable local SQL joins without cross-shard RPC overhead.
commonPitfalls: Sharding different tables on different keys, forcing cross-shard distributed joins.
